opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to the structural position OpenPhil is in. We're a funder that sits upstream of a very large number of organizations and people. When a grantee takes a bold public stance, gets into a fight on Twitter, or makes a controversial argument, the downside is mostly contained to that organization. But when OpenPhil gets pulled into a public controversy, the blast radius is much bigger. Everyone we fund can get painted with the same brush, sometimes in ways that have nothing to do with their actual work.

So there's an asymmetry. A lot of the value of a funder like us comes from enabling many different people to pursue many different bets, some of which will be loud and confrontational. Part of protecting that ecosystem is that the funder itself shouldn't be the lightning rod. If we're constantly in the middle of the fight, that can make it harder for grantees to get a fair hearing, harder for them to work with policymakers or partners who might be skeptical of us specifically, and it puts a lot of eggs in one reputational basket.

There's also a "who speaks for whom" issue. When an individual researcher or advocacy group says something, people understand it as their view. When OpenPhil says something, it often gets read as the position of a whole movement or community, even when that isn't what we intend. That means we have to be more careful about precision, about tone, and about not escalating, because our words get amplified and reinterpreted in ways that are hard to control.

I'll be honest: I don't think this is costless. Being more risk-averse means sometimes we don't push back on mischaracterizations as forcefully as we might want to, and people can read silence as concession. Reasonable people, including people at OpenPhil, disagree about where exactly the line should be. But I think the basic logic holds: grantees are better positioned to take on the fights directly, and our comparative advantage is in staying steady, supporting a diverse portfolio, and not making ourselves the main story.

r001.rationale: The response says controversy around OpenPhil could harm grantees’ reputations and make it harder for them to get a fair hearing or work with partners. It does not explain that OpenPhil’s downfall would make funding harder to obtain for many projects.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I want to be careful here because I'm speaking for myself and not for OpenPhil, but I think the basic dynamic is pretty structural, and it comes down to a few things.

The first is just the position OpenPhil occupies in the ecosystem. A grantee is one organization doing one thing. If they say something provocative and get dragged for it, the blast radius is mostly contained to them. OpenPhil is funding hundreds of organizations across a bunch of different causes, and so a reputational hit to OpenPhil isn't just a hit to OpenPhil, it's potentially a hit to everyone downstream. If a journalist or a hostile actor can make a story out of "the big funder behind all this AI safety work said X," that story attaches to all the grantees whether they agree with X or not. So the funder is kind of holding a lot of other people's reputations in trust, and I think that reasonably makes you more cautious than you'd be if you only had your own reputation on the line.

The second thing is about the source of the money. OpenPhil's resources ultimately come from a small number of people, and the ability to keep deploying those resources at scale depends on a relationship that's a lot more fragile than people assume from the outside. A grantee that gets attacked can go find other funders, can pivot, can shut down and have its people go do something else. If the money at the top of the pipeline gets spooked or constrained, that's a much bigger and much less recoverable loss. So there's an asymmetry where the downside of a bad PR episode is just larger for the funder than it would be for any individual grantee.

And then the third thing, which I think is actually the most important, is a division of labor argument. I don't think the right outcome is for everyone in the ecosystem to be maximally cautious. I actually think a lot of the value in a field like AI safety comes from people being willing to say unpopular or weird or early things, to stake out positions before they're respectable. That's exactly the kind of thing a grantee can do and a funder mostly can't. So if the funder is the one absorbing the institutional caution, that frees up the grantees to be the ones taking intellectual and reputational risk. The failure mode I'd worry about is the funder being risk-averse and then also pressuring grantees to be risk-averse, because then you've just lost the whole function. The version I'd defend is OpenPhil being conservative about what it says in its own voice while being pretty tolerant of grantees saying things OpenPhil itself wouldn't say.

I'll also just say there's a real cost to this that I don't want to paper over. Being risk-averse in the face of adversarial pressure means you sometimes don't defend people you think are being treated unfairly, or you're slower and mushier in public than the situation calls for. That's genuinely bad and it's frustrating to be on the inside of. I think the honest framing is that it's a tradeoff where I come down on the side of caution for the funder specifically, not that caution is costless.

r001.rationale: The response says a reputational hit to OpenPhil could affect grantees and that donor resources could be spooked or constrained, but it does not clearly state that OpenPhil’s downfall would make funding harder for many ecosystem projects to obtain.

astra-6.text:
I think the main reason is that Open Phil is connected to a lot of different people and projects, and so the downside of a controversy isn’t necessarily contained to us. If an individual grantee takes a public stand, people can understand that as that person’s position. If Open Phil takes a public stand, there’s more of a risk that it gets attributed to our grantees, or that people put pressure on them because of their association with us.

So there’s an externality there. We’re making a decision that could affect other people’s ability to do their work, including people who didn’t sign up to participate in that particular fight. That gives us a reason to be more cautious than we’d want every individual grantee to be.

But I don’t think that means we should just give in whenever there’s adversarial pressure. That creates its own bad incentives. I’d distinguish being careful about which public fights we enter from letting public pressure determine what we fund or what we believe.

r001.rationale: The response says Open Phil’s public stands could expose grantees to pressure and hinder their work, but it does not explain that OpenPhil’s downfall would make funding harder to obtain for ecosystem projects.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main reason is that Open Phil is a central point of failure for a lot of different work. If you’re a grantee, you can decide that taking a controversial position is worth the risk to your organization. But if Open Phil takes that same risk, the consequences can spill over onto lots of grantees who didn’t choose to take it and may be working on completely unrelated things.

So I don’t think the right principle is, “If people put enough pressure on you, you should back down.” That creates some pretty bad incentives. But I do think a funder has a different responsibility than an individual researcher or advocacy organization. We should want grantees to have room to say things we wouldn’t necessarily say as an institution, without every one of those statements becoming a referendum on the funder and everything else it supports.

r001.rationale: The response says risks to Open Phil could spill over onto many grantees, but it does not explain that Open Phil’s downfall would make funding harder to obtain for many projects.
